questions.question: In the spiral view of requirements engineering, which activity directly follows “Requirements elicitation”?
questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Easy] The spiral diagram shows that after requirements elicitation the next step is user validation of requirements [Page 12].

---

questions.question: According to Figure 4.7, which of the following is NOT one of the three main phases of the requirements elicitation and analysis process?
questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] Figure 4.7 lists discovery, documentation, and prioritization as the three phases; testing and deployment are not included [Page 13].

---

questions.question: Which statement best captures the purpose of requirements validation as described in the text?

options.A: To create detailed design specifications for developers.
options.B: To ensure the documented requirements reflect the customer’s true needs.
options.C: To prioritize requirements based on stakeholder importance.
options.D: To transform business requirements into user interface mock‑ups.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] Validation is defined as checking that requirements define the system the customer really wants, i.e., they reflect true needs [Page 29].

---

questions.question: In the context of requirements elicitation, which activity would most likely involve constructing a low‑fidelity model to gather stakeholder feedback?
questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] The spiral view lists “Prototyping” as an activity associated with elicitation, used to obtain feedback [Page 12].

---

questions.question: If a project team discovers conflicting stakeholder needs during the “Requirements prioritization and negotiation” phase, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Proceed directly to system design ignoring the conflict.
options.B: Conduct a feasibility study to eliminate one stakeholder.
options.C: Negotiate and reach a consensus on requirement importance.
options.D: Document the conflict without resolution and continue.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] The prioritization and negotiation phase is intended to resolve conflicts by negotiating requirement importance [Page 13].

---

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the relationship between requirements elicitation and validation?

options.A: Validation occurs only after all requirements have been implemented.
options.B: Validation is a separate process that does not overlap with elicitation.
options.C: Validation overlaps with elicitation and analysis to find problems early.
options.D: Validation replaces the need for any stakeholder interviews.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] The text states that validation overlaps with elicitation and analysis, focusing on finding problems with the requirements [Page 29].

---

questions.question: During the “Requirements discovery and understanding” phase, which technique would most directly help uncover hidden user needs?

options.C: Creating a detailed data flow diagram
options.D: Performing code reviews of existing systems

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] Discovery and understanding involve techniques like interviews and observation to reveal hidden needs, as implied by the phase’s purpose [Page 13].

---

questions.question: In the spiral model, what is the primary purpose of the “Feasibility” start point before entering the requirements activities?

options.A: To validate each requirement with the customer.
options.B: To assess whether the proposed system can be built within constraints.
options.C: To prioritize requirements based on cost.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] The “Feasibility” step initiates the process by evaluating whether the system is viable within given constraints [Page 12].

---

questions.question: Which of the following is a direct output of the “Requirements documentation, classification and organization” phase?

options.A: A prototype used for stakeholder review.
options.B: A prioritized list of requirements with stakeholder agreements.
options.C: A structured requirements specification organized by type (business, user, system).
options.D: A feasibility report evaluating technical risks.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] This phase produces a structured specification that classifies requirements into business, user, and system categories as shown in the diagram [Page 12].

---

questions.question: When performing requirements validation, which activity would most likely reveal that a requirement is too ambiguous?

options.A: Tracing the requirement to a specific business goal.
options.B: Conducting a peer review of the requirement wording.
options.C: Estimating the development effort for the requirement.
options.D: Mapping the requirement to a prototype feature.

questions.explanation: [Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] Peer reviews aim to detect ambiguities and inconsistencies, aligning with the validation goal of finding problems in requirements [Page 29].
